Summary  
This seminar paper analyses how the use of machine-learning systems in government agencies can undermine democratic legitimacy when their decisions violate Thomas Christiano’s publicity/​public-equality principle. It catalogues the multiple kinds of opacity (observational, theoretical, proprietary, sociological, psychological) that make it hard for citizens and courts to obtain case-specific reasons, illustrates resulting failures with the COMPAS recidivism tool and a Swedish Public Employment Agency pilot, and sketches conditions under which ML could still be legitimate (low-stakes decisions, effective human override, robust appeals, high transparency).  

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[83] – Nodes and edges follow required patterns, all reasoning paths are connected, no node is isolated and no intervention links directly to a risk.  

Inference strategy  
• Whenever the text recommended a condition (“must allow appeal”, “should disclose code”) it was converted into a concrete intervention node.  
• Where only anecdotal evidence was provided, confidence was set to 2–3.  
• Section headers were approximated from presenter slides (“Democratic legitimacy & principle of publicity”, “Machine learning in public decision making”, etc.) for traceability.  

Extraction completeness  
The fabric captures each causal chain the paper offers: from the top-level risk of illegitimate coercive power → opacity and statistical similarity problems → theoretical claims about publicity and stakes → design rationales (human oversight, restricted deployment) → concrete mechanisms (transparency audits, explainable models, appeals) → validation evidence (COMPAS case, Swedish agency case) → five actionable interventions.  

Key limitations  
• Validation evidence is anecdotal rather than experimental; edge confidences are therefore medium.  
• Paper offered no quantitative results, so validation nodes remain qualitative.  
• Some section titles were inferred because the transcript lacked explicit slide headings.
